title: What’s Actually in Your Moisturizer? Using Ingredient Data to Predict Consumer Satisfaction
text:
The Research Question
Can ingredient composition, price point, and product category predict consumer satisfaction scores in the personal care market?

title: What’s Actually in Your Moisturizer? Using Ingredient Data to Predict Consumer Satisfaction
text:
My Goals

Collect live product and ingredient data from Sephora using a two-stage scraping pipeline
Build a reusable Python package (ingredientparser) to parse and structure raw cosmetic ingredient strings
Train and compare classification models to predict high vs. low consumer satisfaction
Publish a fully reproducible pipeline to GitHub

title: What’s Actually in Your Moisturizer? Using Ingredient Data to Predict Consumer Satisfaction
text:
Data
Data will be collected via Apify scrapers targeting Sephora’s skincare catalog, capturing product attributes, pricing, ratings, and ingredient lists across approximately 2,600 products.

title: Building the Pipeline: From Raw Scrape to Modeling-Ready Data
text:
In my first post, I introduced the question driving this project: can ingredient composition, price point, and product category predict consumer satisfaction in the personal care market? Before I could touch a single model, though, I had to answer a much less glamorous question first: how do you actually get clean, structured data out of a beauty retailer’s website?
This post walks through that journey — from raw scraped HTML to a modeling-ready table sitting in Unity Catalog. If you’ve ever tried to turn messy real-world data into something a model can use, a lot of this will probably sound familiar.

title: Building the Pipeline: From Raw Scrape to Modeling-Ready Data
text:
Stage 1: Scraping Sephora with Apify
I used Apify to collect data in two stages, because Sephora’s product pages and ingredient/review data live behind different scraping logic.
Stage one pulled basic product listings — names, brands, prices, and category info — across the site. Stage two went deeper, pulling ingredient lists and review data for each individual product.
The two-stage approach made sense conceptually, but it came with a real-world wrinkle: the ingredient-scraping actor silently dropped a meaningful chunk of submitted URLs on every run, with no error message to explain why. There was no clean way to predict which URLs would get skipped — it just happened, quietly, every time.
The fix wasn’t elegant, but it worked: I reran the scrape multiple times, each time checking which products were still missing ingredient data, until I’d captured roughly 96.5% of the catalog. The remaining gap turned out to mostly be discontinued products that had likely been pulled from the site entirely, which made sense.
Takeaway: when a scraping tool fails silently, build your pipeline to expect partial results and make rerunning safe, rather than assuming one pass will get you everything.

title: Building the Pipeline: From Raw Scrape to Modeling-Ready Data
text:
Stage 2: Idempotent Ingestion into Databricks
That last point — making reruns safe — became the design principle for how I loaded data into Unity Catalog.
Early on, I was tempted to just overwrite tables on every run. But once I started rerunning scrapes to catch missing ingredient data, a plain overwrite would have meant redoing work I’d already done, or worse, losing data I already had if a partial rerun failed midway.
Instead, I built the ingestion pipeline around a simple idea: only insert what’s actually new. Concretely, that meant:

Using a LEFT JOIN against the existing table to identify which incoming rows weren’t already present
Using MERGE statements so reruns update or insert records without duplicating anything

This made the whole pipeline idempotent — I could rerun the same ingestion script as many times as I needed (which, given the Apify dropout issue, I needed to do a lot) without worrying about duplicate rows or accidentally clobbering good data.
I also hit a more mundane technical snag along the way: Delta tables would throw a DELTA_METADATA_MISMATCH error whenever I tried to write a dataframe with a slightly different schema than what already existed (for instance, after adding a new column). The fix was adding .option("overwriteSchema", "true") to the write call — a small thing, but one of those errors that’s confusing the first time you hit it and trivial once you know the fix.

title: Building the Pipeline: From Raw Scrape to Modeling-Ready Data
text:
Stage 3: Cleaning the Ingredient Strings
Once the raw data was sitting in Unity Catalog, I ran into the messiest part of the whole project: the ingredient strings themselves.
I expected something like a clean, comma-separated INCI list — Water, Glycerin, Niacinamide, … — for every product. What I actually got was a mix of real ingredient lists tangled up with marketing copy, like:

“Ectoin: A super humectant promotes refreshed, healthy-looking skin… -Hexapeptide: A six-amino acid peptide helps reduce the appearance of age-related changes…”

Several attempts to clean this didn’t quite work. Anchoring on common starter words like “Aqua” or “Water” failed because plenty of legitimate ingredient lists start with something else entirely (one product’s actual first ingredient was Squalane). Splitting on punctuation patterns like periods and dashes also backfired — it occasionally chopped off real ingredient names that happened to look like the end of a marketing sentence.
The approach that finally worked was based on a different signal entirely: structure, not content. Marketing copy reads like sentences — verbs, articles, descriptive language. INCI ingredient lists read like a tightly packed sequence of short, capitalized chemical names separated by commas. So instead of looking for specific anchor words, I used a regular expression that looks for a long run of comma-separated, capitalized tokens — and treats that run as the “real” ingredient list, discarding anything that came before it.
It’s not a perfect solution (no regex-based approach to natural-language-adjacent text ever fully is), but it cleanly separated marketing copy from ingredient data across the vast majority of the catalog.

title: Building the Pipeline: From Raw Scrape to Modeling-Ready Data
section: Stage 4: Turning Text into Features with ingredientparser
text:
Stage 4: Turning Text into Features with ingredientparser
With clean(er) ingredient strings in hand, the next step was turning raw text into something a model could actually use. That’s the job of ingredientparser, a small Python package I built specifically for this project.
At its core, ingredientparser does two things:

Cleans raw ingredient strings using the structural approach described above
Extracts structured features from the cleaned list — things like ingredient count, whether the product contains specific actives (retinol, niacinamide, hyaluronic acid, vitamin C, and others), and whether it contains common irritants like fragrance

I cross-referenced ingredient names against CosDNA and INCIDecoder to make sure the actives and irritants I was flagging matched real formulation science, rather than just guessing based on what sounded familiar.
Packaging this as a proper, installable Python library (rather than a one-off script) turned out to matter more than I expected. It meant I could install it consistently across notebooks, write actual unit tests against it, and — eventually — install it directly from a private GitHub repository rather than relying on file-path hacks. I’ll get into the details of that packaging journey in a future post, since it deserves its own write-up.

title: Building the Pipeline: From Raw Scrape to Modeling-Ready Data
text:
What’s Next
At this point, I had a clean, structured, feature-rich dataset sitting in Unity Catalog — ready for the part of the project I’d actually signed up for: modeling. In my next post, I’ll walk through how I built the binary satisfaction label, trained and compared three classification models, and the (genuinely surprising) finding about what actually predicts consumer satisfaction in this dataset.

title: Teaching a Model to Read an Ingredient List
text:
If you flip a moisturizer over, the ingredient list looks like this:
That’s a paragraph of text. A model can’t do anything with a paragraph — it needs numbers. Getting from one to the other is called feature engineering, and it’s where a surprising amount of this project’s real work lived. This post is about how I turned an ingredient list (plus a price and a brand) into 25 numbers a model could actually learn from.

title: Teaching a Model to Read an Ingredient List
section: The problem: ingredient lists are text, not data
text:
The problem: ingredient lists are text, not data
Every product in my dataset came with a raw INCI string — the standardized ingredient list. To compare products, I needed consistent, numeric answers to questions like: How many ingredients does it have? Does it contain a known active like niacinamide or retinol? How many potential irritants? Is there added fragrance?
Doing that by hand across 2,201 products wasn’t happening. So I built a small tool to do it.

title: Teaching a Model to Read an Ingredient List
text:
The ingredientparser package
Rather than bury this logic in a notebook cell, I packaged it. ingredientparser takes a raw ingredient string and returns a structured set of features:
from ingredientparser import parse_ingredients

features = parse_ingredients("Water, Glycerin, Niacinamide, Retinol, Fragrance")

# {
#   "ingredient_count": 5,
#   "has_niacinamide": 1,
#   "has_retinol": 1,
#   "has_hyaluronic_acid": 0,
#   "has_vitamin_c": 0,
#   "active_count": 2,
#   "irritant_count": 1,
#   "has_fragrance": 1,
# }
The “known actives” and “irritants” it looks for come from reference lists I built using CosDNA and INCIDecoder, so the flags reflect how the skincare world actually categorizes ingredients.
I made it a proper package rather than a loose function on purpose. It has a src/ layout, a pyproject.toml, and a small pytest suite, and it lives in a GitHub repo. That means I can install it straight into Databricks from the repo, version it, and hand it to someone else without copying and pasting code. For a project meant to be reproducible, that mattered more than it might sound — it turned a one-off script into a reusable piece of infrastructure.

title: Teaching a Model to Read an Ingredient List
text:
Beyond ingredients: engineering more signal
Ingredients are only part of a product. So I built out three more groups of features.
Price. Beyond the raw low and high price, I added a price_range (the spread between them) and a value_tier that buckets products into budget, mid, and luxury, then one-hot encoded it.
df["price_range"] = df["high_price"] - df["low_price"]
Interactions. Some things might matter more in combination than alone. For example, a bestseller that also contains an active, or niacinamide without fragrance (a combination that tends to signal a more clinical, sensitive-skin-friendly formula).
df["niacinamide_no_fragrance"] = df["has_niacinamide"] * (1 - df["has_fragrance"])
Brand signals. This is the group that ended up mattering most — though I didn’t know that yet. Using a hand-curated reference file, I added whether a brand is celebrity-owned or dermatologist-owned, and the brand’s Instagram follower count.

title: Teaching a Model to Read an Ingredient List
text:
The final roster: 25 features
Grouped, the model’s inputs looked like this:

Formulation: ingredient count, has retinol / niacinamide / hyaluronic acid / vitamin C, active count, irritant count, has fragrance
Product: low and high price, bestseller, new, Sephora-exclusive, online-only
Engineered: price range, value tier (budget / mid / luxury), and the interaction features
Brand signal: Instagram followers, celebrity-owned, dermatologist-owned

title: Teaching a Model to Read an Ingredient List
section: What I expected — and a hint of what happened
text:
What I expected — and a hint of what happened
Going in, my money was on the formulation features. It seemed obvious: a well-formulated product with the right actives and no irritants should earn happier customers. That was the whole premise.
The model had other ideas. When I trained it and looked at what it actually leaned on, the formulation features — the ones I’d spent the most effort building — barely moved the needle. The brand signals did.
That’s the subject of the next post.

title: What Actually Predicts Whether You’ll Love a Skincare Product
text:
Here’s the short version, since it surprised me too: across 2,201 Sephora skincare products, a brand’s Instagram following predicted customer satisfaction better than its ingredients or its price — and the relationship runs backwards. The smaller the following, the happier the customers.
This post is how I got there.

title: What Actually Predicts Whether You’ll Love a Skincare Product
text:
The question, and the label
The whole project asked one thing: can what a product is made of, what it costs, and the brand behind it predict whether customers will be satisfied? To make “satisfied” something a model could learn, I split products into high and low satisfaction at the median rating (4.45), among products with enough reviews to be reliable. That gave a balanced target — roughly a 53/47 split — so the model couldn’t cheat by always guessing one class.

title: What Actually Predicts Whether You’ll Love a Skincare Product
text:
Three models, one winner
I trained three classifiers on the 25 features from the last post and compared them on a held-out test set:



Model
Accuracy
AUC




Logistic regression
0.55
0.590


Random forest
0.66
0.712


Gradient boosting
0.66
0.714



Gradient boosting won, though barely over random forest. The bigger story is the gap between the tree models and logistic regression: a straight-line model could barely beat a coin flip (AUC 0.59), while the tree-based models jumped to ~0.71. That tells you the signal in this data is non-linear — the relationships bend, and only flexible models can follow them.
To make sure that 0.71 wasn’t a lucky test split, I ran 5-fold cross-validation: AUC 0.73 ± 0.04. Steady. And against a majority-class baseline (0.53 accuracy, 0.50 AUC), the model is clearly learning something real, if modest.

title: What Actually Predicts Whether You’ll Love a Skincare Product
section: What the model actually leaned on
text:
What the model actually leaned on
Here’s where the premise fell apart. I expected the formulation features — actives, ingredient count, irritants — to carry the model. They didn’t. When I ranked what the model relied on, one feature towered over everything:



SHAP feature importance — brand Instagram followers dominates, with ingredients and price far behind.


Brand Instagram followers accounted for about 44% of the model’s decisions. Low price came next at ~17%, ingredient count at ~10%, and everything else trailed off. The ingredient features I’d spent the most effort building were near the bottom.
Even more interesting than which feature mattered was which direction it pushed. Using SHAP values to read the model’s logic, the effect of followers is inverse: more followers pushed predictions toward lower satisfaction.

title: What Actually Predicts Whether You’ll Love a Skincare Product
text:
The twist, in one chart
Grouping brands by follower count makes it plain:



High-satisfaction rate falls as brand following grows.


Brands with under 100K followers earned high satisfaction 82% of the time. For the biggest brands — over 10M followers — that dropped to 38%. The steepest fall happens early: even a modest jump in fame comes with a satisfaction cost.

title: What Actually Predicts Whether You’ll Love a Skincare Product
text:
Why would that be?
Worth being clear: my model shows a pattern, not a cause. It can’t tell me why smaller brands score higher. But a likely driver is audience fit. A niche brand’s customers usually sought it out — they researched it, they wanted that specific product. Big-brand products get bought on impulse or by people they were never really for, which means more mismatched, disappointed reviewers. A product with a few hundred reviews from devotees will read very differently than one with tens of thousands from the general public.
I also checked whether the finding was fragile. Tightening the definition of “satisfied” to only the top tier of ratings didn’t break it — brand following still led, and ranking performance actually rose. The pattern holds however strictly you define success.

title: What Actually Predicts Whether You’ll Love a Skincare Product
text:
So what?
The project started from a practical question: how does a new company know whether a product will land well before it launches? The honest answer this data gives is a little humbling and a little encouraging.
Humbling, because satisfaction isn’t something you can reliably engineer in the formula. Stacking on actives or pricing a certain way didn’t separate the winners.
Encouraging, because for a small or new brand, being small isn’t a disadvantage here — if anything, it lines up with the outcome you want. The thing a newcomer lacks, a giant following, is the very thing associated with lower satisfaction.
None of this proves that buying followers would tank your ratings, or that going viral dooms a product. It’s correlation, on one retailer, at one moment in time, from a model that’s a useful lens rather than a crystal ball. But as a lens, it points somewhere genuinely counterintuitive: in skincare, who makes a product predicts satisfaction better than what’s in it.
